en: She herself was still a young child,
Her hair not yet long enough to braid,
In a red dress with a crescent waist.
From the shimmering beauties
She had gathered the finest.
Upon a wondrous plane tree and birch
They had hung the swing.
She appeared like a noble maiden;
Poor Churok stood at their head,
And thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens
Had begun their games.
In their midst, your sister-in-law
Played and raised laughter.
With renowned Churok at their head,
The companion watching them
Felt his heart carried away.
Kulchoro, who had never seen a maiden,
Saw them and grew excited;
He began the whole commotion.
With red Buurul beneath him,
Kulchoro turned at an angle
The fearsome Urgench—
He plunged straight into it.
Kulchoro had seen the maidens;
The poor man, who had never seen a maiden,
Did not look all around him,
And in the fearsome Urgench
Did not spare his threadlike life.
They set aside the swing,

en: And played the game of Shabiyet;
Maidens and daughters-in-law mingled,
With mighty Churok at their head,
And played their difficult game.
Flattering Churok,
They excitedly told their dreams,
That lively Akylay of before
Spoke of an auspicious sign:
"My dear elder sisters,
My honored sisters-in-law,
Last night as I slept, I dreamed;
In my dream I saw a fortunate sign.
A black-spotted tiger
Ranged through the city,
And the dogs would not stop their sharp barking.
A scarred gray-wolf lion
Came raging into Afghanistan;
Such good fortune appeared.
Saying, 'I shall go out to meet him,'
The enemies who opposed him were destroyed;
Saying, 'This is that black-spotted tiger,'
The people of Afghanistan honored him.
What can this mean?
Younger sister and elder sister,
Interpret this dream of mine!
A giant black bird, the Zymyruk,
Stretched its great feet down from the sky.
Unable to withstand its wrath,
The besieging Jediger
Fled away like crows.
Forty men, each worth a thousand,
Within this city of Afghanistan
Established their royal camp firmly;
They took everything in the direction they faced.
What can this mean?
Interpret this dream of mine!"
While Akylay stood speaking thus,
Bold Kynymjan began to speak:
"That black-spotted tiger
Was my khanly brother-in-law Semetey himself.
He will grasp his blood-drinking weapon
Because of my honored elder sister,
And cast havoc
Among the enemies who oppose him.
The scarred gray-wolf lion,
Who burns everything he faces,
Was my heroic brother-in-law himself;
From Kojo, who brought disaster,
He will deliver us.
The giant black bird, the Zymyruk,
Stretching its feet down from the sky,
From his father, gray-wolf Manas,
My elder sister's husband
Was born to surpass him, we have heard.
My tiger brother-in-law, that gray wolf,
Will come here himself;
If an enemy comes out to fight,
He will cast havoc among them.
A husband has come
For my renowned, unfortunate sister!"
Before she finished telling her dream,
The dark-haired maiden posted as lookout,
And the fair-haired maiden set as guard,
Bent their knees,
Bowed before Aychurok,
And shouted out their good news:
"Thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens,
Women playing your games,
Come here!" they called.
"My dear elder sisters!
Did you learn what I learned?
Did you perceive what I perceived?
Did you see what I saw?
A man has come to the farther bank,
His enormity equal to half a mountain,
As though he would devour all he sees.
He is broad across the right shoulder;
When I look at his bearing,
He is a hero who could rout the Oyrat.
He rides the red horse Buurul,
Its horsehair tail tied in a firm knot;
He is girded with a silver belt,
And turns a face radiant as the sun;
He wears a bulletproof coat,
He rides a horse no bullet can overtake;
He is himself a surpassing giant,
The very image of my brother-in-law.
Ruddy-cheeked and imposing of face,
He is a mass of glowing red embers;
No one like him exists in the world.
He is my brother-in-law himself,
For my poor, surpassing elder sister,
The time has come for him to embrace her.
He wears a coat with a golden collar
And rides mountain-like Buurul.
A banner can be seen in his hand;
The sight opens the heart.
He is my khanly brother-in-law himself,
Out upon the games in the field,
To my elder sister, without growing weary,
The time has come for him to meet her!
When they heard this news,
Thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens,
With Aychurok in their midst,
All leaned out and stared
At the one who had come to the farther bank.
Saying, "Our wondrous brother-in-law has come,"
Thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens
Leaned out and watched with delight.
Those who did not know began to speak:
"It is our brother-in-law himself;
If not himself, it is his very dark eye.
Having tired his horse and scouted the road,
He has come from far away;
It is our lion brother-in-law himself!"
While the maidens and daughters-in-law spoke thus,
Your precious Churok said this:
"You grew in a desert no person ever saw—
Damn your fathers' graves, maidens and brides—
And stand astonished by this creature.
He scouts the crossing with a haughty air.
Your brother-in-law is not one who would come first;
He is not the one who would come first,
Nor some clumsy, staggering boy
Who would scout the ford himself!
You opium-assed waddlers,
You wretches who have never seen a man!
What will you do when you see his young one?
You would mount his companion;
What will you do when you see the great one?
You would mount the little fry;
What will you do when you see the great catfish?
With a face like oiled wheat,
And eyes like twilight mist,
His enormity equal to half a mountain,
As though he would devour all he sees—
What will you do when you see your lord?
Have you heard the tale?
Long ago my father-in-law, the heroic lion,
Lived many years without seeing a child;
At first he remained childless,
Then saw his gray wolf son
At fifty-two years of age.
Saying, 'At last I have seen my son,'
My heroic father-in-law who has passed
Slaughtered ninety beasts for his feast.
Giant Koshoy of the unseen gave the name,
And he received the name Semetey.
When the child was newly born,
Making plans of surpassing greatness,
Infidel and Muslim alike,
They summoned everyone without exception,
And held an extraordinary feast.
The people gathered for his feast;
The Russians ate of his feast and departed,
Saying, 'If this child lives,
He will rout the Oyrat.'
The Chinese ate of his feast and departed,
Saying, 'If this child lives,
He will throw the age into turmoil.'
When provoked to vengeance,
He struck down his own elder brother,
That true gray wolf, born imperious,
Is not your brother-in-law himself!
You babbling poor women,
How much must I tell you?
If you ask the lineage
Of the young man on the farther bank:
Long ago, when my gray-wolf father-in-law,
That hero,
Was in the fullness of his time,
The father of the young man across the river,
A gray-wolf lion,
Strayed from the straight road.
He bitterly contested
The khanship of Kakan-Chyn and Beijing;
Barely escaping death,
He fought with his own close kinsmen.
His heart turned away from the Chinese,
And he migrated from Beijing.
He found a land like broad Talas
And a hero like my father-in-law;
He rendered true and surpassing service,
And his purpose brought good fortune.
This is the son left as a legacy
By a lord like Almambet.
If you saw the son, you would bow;
If you saw the hero, you would tremble."
Churok spoke and fell silent.
The maidens and daughters-in-law grew enamored
Of the young man across the river;
The thought, "If only he were my husband,"
Brought great trouble into their minds.
The maidens and daughters-in-law marveled greatly
At the young man on the farther bank.
They gazed at him with longing,
Placed wishing necklaces around their necks,
And, for the young man on the farther bank,
Saying, "If only he were my husband,"
All the maidens and daughters-in-law
Made their wishes in agitation:
"If only Argyn and Kyrgyz gathered
And camped on both banks;
If only that dear young man
Were an honored lover and companion
Among our people.
To the young man standing across the river,
May this dark life God created for me
Become a sacrifice."
All the maidens and daughters-in-law
Leaned out, staring in wonder.
Some maidens said,
"If only that young man across the river
Were the one I took as husband."
Others spoke and said,
"That howling, ill-fated wretch
Is a shameless poor man."
All the maidens cried out together
And entered into the clamor;
They fell into an immense uproar
That would not subside.
Some of them said,
"The moment he crosses, he will die."
Others spoke and said,
"Will he take his own life?
Will God strike the young man?
He will turn back."
